title: What time is the 2026 Mexico City GP and how can I watch it?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 season heads to Mexico City next for the 19th race weekend of the campaign, with the drivers barely having time to catch their breath after racing in Austin last Sunday.

Kimi Antonelli took the victory at the Circuit of The Americas in dominant fashion for Mercedes, leaving him on the cusp of a historic Drivers’ title, which he looks likely to wrap up at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

George Russell and Lewis Hamilton are the only two who can stop the Italian, but both will need to win this weekend to stand any chance of keeping their title hopes alive.

Head to the RACE HUB or scroll down for more on how and when you can watch the action, along with the global start times for each session.

What time is the Mexico City Grand Prix?

The weekend will kick off with Free Practice 1 at 1230 local time on Friday, 30 October, followed by Free Practice 2 later that day at 1600.

A final hour of practice will begin at 1130 on Saturday, 31 October, before Qualifying gets underway at 1500. The Grand Prix itself will take place at 1400 on Sunday, 01 November.

Check out the image below to find all the global start times for Sunday’s race.

How can I watch the Mexico City Grand Prix?

You can enjoy coverage from every session live on F1 TV Pro (available in selected countries), which brings fans closer to the action via exclusive features like onboard cameras on all 22 of the drivers’ cars, and access to both Pre-Race and Post-Race Shows.

F1 TV Pro can be streamed easily via Apple TV, Chromecast Generation 2 and above, Android TV, Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Roku. F1 TV Pro is free of ad breaks and available with commentary in six languages.

Fans can also watch via F1 TV Premium, a premier service that invites fans to step into the heart of the action with the ability to watch races in 4K Ultra HD/HDR on up to six different devices, as well as a personalised Multiview feature available on select devices with 26 different feeds to choose from.

Viewers can watch every F1 Grand Prix, F1 Sprint, Qualifying and practice session live in 4K Ultra HD/HDR at home, with F2, F3, F1 ACADEMY and Porsche Supercup sessions also available to watch live on the platform.

Alternatively, live timing will be available on F1.com and the F1 app across every session during the Grand Prix weekend.

Where is the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix taking place?

The Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez will host the 19th Grand Prix of the season, a track renowned for its atmosphere with the event often happening alongside the national holiday of Dia de Muertos.

This iconic circuit returned to the calendar in 2015, and has become a fan favourite ever since.

From the long start/finish straight to the raucous stadium section, the circuit offers plenty of character and makes for a breathless experience given its high altitude, which requires some lateral thinking from the teams in terms of car and brake cooling.

What is the weather forecast in Mexico City?

The weekend looks set to be warm and sunny, with temperatures just a few degrees cooler than the drivers enjoyed in Austin.

But there could be some showers around for Friday practice, so the teams will keep an eye on the skies to see if those materialise. The weather is generally good in Mexico, so whether that threat recedes and all three days of track action are run in sunny conditions remains to be seen.

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Austin?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli took another step towards the 2026 world title with a superb display at the Circuit of The Americas in Austin. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges?

Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Antonelli delivered a Qualifying and Grand Prix performance worthy of a World Champion last weekend – charging to both pole position and the race win. Despite Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc’s best efforts, the young Italian was simply unstoppable, and he now has another finger on the 2026 Drivers’ Championship trophy.

As the wait goes on to find out if he will keep his seat for 2027, Liam Lawson made another statement to Red Bull and Racing Bulls chiefs in the United States with his latest Q3 showing and points result. He has now scored in 13 of the 17 Grands Prix he has finished this year, and only appears to be growing in confidence and maturity.

After topping Friday practice and leading the way in Q2, Leclerc was left searching for answers when he ended up P4 in Qualifying – track conditions appearing to move away from Ferrari at the critical moment. He made up for it at the race start by passing Isack Hadjar off the line and then Verstappen with a bold move through the esses, and ended the day as Antonelli’s nearest challenger.

Verstappen arrived in Austin off the back of victories in Malaysia and Singapore, and he seemed to be in the mix for another win when he qualified on the front row of the grid. Race day was more of a challenge for the Dutchman, though, with a compromised start, a tyre strategy that he openly questioned and various technical issues. Nonetheless, he battled on and came away with a podium.

Pierre Gasly continued to wring the neck of Alpine’s package at the Circuit of The Americas, with the Frenchman getting close to Q3 in Qualifying and taking the fight to the cars ahead on race day. A well-earned point, which denied Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg and the other Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad, was his reward this time out – even after picking up damage in a scrap with Haas’ Ollie Bearman (for which the latter earned a penalty).

Lewis Hamilton started Sunday’s race from fifth position, just behind team mate Leclerc, but lost ground to the front-runners in the opening stint after lining up with used tyres – the only driver in the field to do so. His “biggest issue” as the encounter progressed, however, was the SF-26’s balance feeling “off”. A more competitive final stint saw him close back in on the podium places, but he ultimately had to settle for fourth.

Hadjar was one of the stars of Qualifying at the Circuit of The Americas with his P3 effort – sorting out an “undriveable” Red Bull in Friday practice to finish just a few hundredths down on team mate Verstappen. Unfortunately for the Frenchman, after that strong recovery, “everything went wrong” in the race. Like Verstappen, he was left frustrated by a sluggish start, before getting stuck in an incorrect engine map following a pit stop, which heavily compromised his pace en route to a P6 result.

You could forgive Hulkenberg for having nightmares about the number 11 this season – given how many times he has finished there in Qualifying sessions and Grands Prix. After coming close to Q3, and putting up a spirited midfield fight on race day, 11th proved to be the maximum for the German. It was another very solid performance, though, as Audi continue to lay foundations for the future.

Lando Norris was a man of few words after a track limits violation left him eighth on the grid for the United States Grand Prix – the McLaren man stating that he did a “c*** job”. He managed to make some progress during the race to turn that into a more respectable fifth position, comfortably ahead of team mate Oscar Piastri, as both drivers stuck it out on ageing tyres and adopted a one-stop strategy.

Despite some pre-race technical concerns over his car, Fernando Alonso enjoyed a strong start to Sunday’s Grand Prix – rising from 15th to 12th and knocking on the door of the points-paying positions. However, in his own words, the damage sustained from contact with Williams’ Alex Albon “compromised everything for us”. Alonso eventually had to pit for a new front wing, which dropped him down the order, but there were at least some performance positives to take away from the weekend.

Lindblad headed into the Austin weekend knowing he would be taking an engine-related grid penalty. That turned a strong P9 on the grid (after team mate Lawson opted against running in Q3) into P14, and left him with an uphill struggle to score points. After early contact with Carlos Sainz’s Williams, he gave it his all to recover the lost ground and make it back into the top-10 positions, but 12th was the limit in a fiercely competitive midfield fight.

Missing out

Just missing out on this week’s Power Rankings leaderboard are Haas’ Esteban Ocon (14th, after clearing team mate Bearman early on) and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto (13th, from a back-of-the-grid engine penalty).

title: Bearman and Gasly reflect on US GP collision
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman and Pierre Gasly have reflected on their collision in the United States Grand Prix, with the former stating "I don't regret going for the move" despite being handed a penalty.

The pair were on the fringes of the top 10 in the early stages of Sunday's race at the Circuit of The Americas, with Bearman having closed up to the Alpine driver as a Virtual Safety Car ended.

Bearman, who had already made up two places on the opening lap, lunged to the inside of Gasly through the right of Turn 13 with the pair making what looked like innocuous contact.

Bearman moved ahead but had suffered extensive damage in the collision, as well as picking up a 10-second penalty for the incident, before the Haas driver eventually retired due to the damage.

"I went up his inside, he saw me because he left space but for me it didn't really feel like enough. It was a bit of space but only half a car and by the time I was committed, I wasn't disappearing," said Bearman.

"So we made a bit of contact, I picked up a huge amount of damage on my car. I probably damaged Pierre's car as well. It was a shame because I felt like I was massively penalised for it and it actually ruined my race to have that amount of damage.

"I was losing a second a lap due to downforce and on top of that, I picked up a penalty. In my view it was a racing incident."

Bearman admitted that he needed to be aggressive as Haas struggle to match the performance of midfield teams such as Alpine and Racing Bulls when fighting for minor points positions.

"To be honest, I don't regret going for the move because at this stage if we don't do something special and get a bit lucky, be a aggressive and go for it, then we're not going to score points because we're not fast enough to do that on merit," added Bearman.

Gasly eventually finished P10, but like Bearman had also suffered damage in the collision which he believes cost him any chance of battling Liam Lawson's Racing Bulls for P9.

"I'm pleased because after the contact with Ollie, we had quite a big damage on the floor," he said.

"It was a small touch honestly and I didn't expect the floor to be that damaged following it. But considering the pace after that and the fact we managed to hold onto P10, it's positive."

He added: "I think [the overtake] was a little optimistic, not crazy, but a little optimistic.

"Unfortunately there was this touch which cost us and cost probably 5-10 seconds of race time following it. It was not ideal, but at the same time, he tried it. It just wasn't the cleanest move."

title: Lawson excited for what’s to come after more points in Austin
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is keen to go racing again at the next two rounds in the latest triple header after securing another points finish at the United States Grand Prix, with the New Zealander feeling in a “good place” following his P9 result.

After lining up as ‘best of the rest’ in ninth place on the grid – behind the Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren drivers – Lawson put in a solid drive to bring his Racing Bulls machine home in the same position.

The 24-year-old spoke highly of how the team had performed across the event at the Circuit of The Americas, with his result boosting the squad’s tally as their hold on P5 in the Teams’ Championship strengthens.

“When everyone finishes, for us it's a P9 or a P10 – that's sort of the best we can do,” said Lawson. “Honestly we executed really well today – we had a great race, so couldn't really do more. Overall it's been a strong weekend.”

When pushed on how encouraging it is for him personally to see his consistent run continue, Lawson responded: “I mean honestly, yeah. I feel good. I felt good all weekend. I’m enjoying driving this car, honestly – it's in a great place at the moment, so I’m excited to go to some more sort of unique tracks now.

“Obviously with Mexico [it’s] very high altitude, and Brazil [is] probably going to be quite bumpy I'm guessing. But yeah, we're in a good place.”

On the other side of the garage, Arvid Lindblad was faced with a more challenging afternoon on Sunday after a five-place grid penalty for using additional power unit elements dropped him down to P14.

He ultimately went on to cross the line in 12th place, leaving him unsure about how to summarise his race.

“It was okay,” the Briton reflected afterwards. “Lap 1 wasn't as good as I'd hoped – obviously I went down the inside, but we all kind of stacked up on top of each other so I wasn't really able to make any ground there.

“And then it was a bit difficult, the first stint, and then the second two stints I think were okay, but obviously I boxed quite early onto the medium [tyre]. I was feeling good for a few laps – I was catching Franco [Colapinto], and then I was basically in Pierre [Gasly's] undercut window so then he held me up. I lost about two seconds in half a lap with him.

“Then I tried to get Pierre and probably pushed a bit too hard, but yeah, it is what it is. I'm not really sure honestly how to reflect on the race. For half of it I didn't really know where I was or what was going on.

“I think I was the only one who tried to do the two-stop – I don't think that worked. It is what it is. I think there were positives, so we'll learn from it, and yeah, big thanks to the team anyway.”

Despite this, Lindblad was pleased to have felt better in the car than at earlier points of the weekend.

“I didn't feel very comfortable going into [it] through most of the practices, but then I felt okay in Quali,” he explained. “Honestly, I felt pretty good in the race as well – probably one of the best feelings I've had in the race so far this year.”

title: 'More than a bad start' cost Audi after another P11 finish
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg finished 11th in Austin as Audi once again came agonisingly close to scoring points. It is the third time in the last four races that the German has come home in P11 – something that has become a theme of Audi’s season as a whole.

The team continue to be in the midfield mix, their last big upgrade package bolted on in Baku propelling them into the fight for points. Despite that however, they have only scored once in the last four Grands Prix – Hulkenberg’s P8 in Singapore delivering four much-needed points to the squad.

Things were always going to be tough at the Circuit of The Americas with Gabriel Bortoleto starting from the back after picking up a raft of penalties for taking on new power unit components, although he should in theory have enough parts in his pool now to make it to the end of the season without further issue.

That left Hulkenberg to fight for points from P11 on the grid, and another poor start made his quest even tougher.

“You can’t call that a bad start, it went into anti-stall so yeah, that’s more than a bad start,” the German said afterwards.

“A strange one as normally the anti-stall kicks in instantly, and I did a few metres and then it kicked in. Sounded and felt a bit odd, but obviously don’t know what happened, [I'm] fresh out of the car so I need to go back and see what happened and why. But of course, it didn’t help our cause for the race.”

Audi have struggled with reliability this season, especially regarding their power unit. As the only team running the Audi PU, they have significantly less data to draw on than the likes of Mercedes and Ferrari, who each supply customer teams.

But while Hulkenberg failed to start two of the first four races, of late the reliability has been much better – Silverstone was the last time he failed to see the chequered flag. But starts remain an issue, with both cars often losing out off the line and leaving them on the back foot.

“You saw again today we were quite close pace-wise with Pierre [Gasly] and with Liam [Lawson], and obviously we came from behind after that start but not sure we could have done a whole lot more from there,” he added.

“It would have all [been] dependent on how with a good start [where] we would have come out, we can only speculate but it is what it is now.”

Audi sit eighth in the Teams' Championship, seven points adrift of Haas in the fight for seventh. While they seem to have the edge on the American team on pace, the opportunities to score are few and far between at the moment.

As for Bortoleto, he enjoyed his afternoon on track, albeit from the back of the field knowing that making it back towards the top 10 would be a tough ask.

“We did a good race, overtook some cars, kept it clean at the same time you know, no damage. I had a bit of fun overtaking people and being out there, trying my best, putting in some good [racing]. Obviously, it is difficult to recover everything starting from the back,” the Brazilian said.

All the key moments from the 2026 United States Grand Prix

He crossed the line 13th, and like his team mate has five P11 results to his name this season. It has been so often the case of close but not close enough for Audi, who have not been helped by Racing Bulls ahead having strong reliability and two drivers in good form.

But all things considered, Audi are enjoying a solid season with the new generation of cars. They have taken the right direction with their upgrades, have an established driver pairing that work well together and have weathered the disruption of Jonathan Wheatley leaving his role as Team Principal.

All of which means the team have a good base from which to launch into 2027, as they try and climb up the order and challenge more consistently for points.

title: Colton Herta set to finally earn superlicence with latest Cadillac F1 outing
excerpt:
Colton Herta is in line to finally receive his F1 superlicence after Cadillac handed him his latest practice outing, this time at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

According to the team, Herta is on 39 superlicence points after his outing in FP1 last week at the United States Grand Prix, with 40 required to finally earn the American his licence to potentially race in F1.

Herta is set for his fifth FP1 outing of the season, and will assume Valtteri Bottas's MAC-26 in Mexico City, as the Finn stands down for the second of his two mandatory sessions this season.

Herta will have driven in all five of Cadillac's FP1 sessions, with rumours growing that he could be line for a race seat if Bottas is not retained for 2027 - with boss Marcin Budkowski not shutting down a potential change in the driver line-up when questioned in Austin.

Herta will be required to complete 100km of running in FP1 at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, equal to 24 laps of the track to earn the point.

He had picked up FP1 points in Barcelona, Hungary, and the United States, but his session in place of Sergio Perez in Italy did not earn the point as he only completed five laps, or 25km, due to technical problems.

After he moved to 39 points with his Austin FP1 outing, a team spokesman indicated to RacingNews365 that it would be "remiss" of the team not to give the Californian an opportunity to finally achieve the superlicence he has long worked for.

A potential move to F1 in 2022 was blocked by the FIA after it did not agree to give Herta a waiver to qualify for a superlicence without the necessary 40 points in a three-year period.

The bulk of Herta's 39 points to date comes from his 2024 IndyCar season when he finished as runner-up to Alex Palou - and earned 30 superlicence points.

Other results in IndyCar and his FP1 outings have pushed him to 39, with the run in Mexico set to bring him to the magical 40 and earn him his superlicence, should he complete that 100km of running.

"Every opportunity to get behind the wheel with the team is valuable, and I’m looking forward to being back in the car in Mexico," he said in the team preview.

"It’s a great chance to keep learning, build my experience in Formula 1 on a new circuit and contribute to the team’s work across the weekend."

title: Liam Lawson given kick in the teeth by former Red Bull advisor Helmut Marko
excerpt:
Helmut Marko has revealed he would choose Nikola Tsolov over Liam Lawson for a Racing Bulls seat next season.

The comments come with Lawson's future at the Faenza-based outfit still unresolved heading into the closing rounds of this year.

Lawson has done a sterling job, however, with the New Zealander the leading driver in the standings behind those racing with the 'big four' teams of Mercedes, Ferrari, McLaren and Red Bull.

Even taking into account the 14 points Lawson scored during his three-race cameo with Red Bull just after the summer break as the replacement for an injured Isack Hadjar, the New Zealander would still be comfortably clear of 10th-placed Pierre Gasly.

Tsolov, meanwhile, is next in line in the Red Bull pipeline. The Bulgarian finished runner-up in last year's F3 championship, and is currently second in this season's F2 with two rounds remaining in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, provided they go ahead.

Marko, the long-time architect of Red Bull's junior programme, has made clear where his sympathies lie when reflecting on the Lawson-Tsolov dilemma.

He has pointed to the junior driver's development in F3 and F2 as proof of Red Bull's long-standing philosophy of promoting its own talent.

Referring initially to Dietrich Mateschitz, the founder of the two F1 teams who passed away in October 2022, speaking to Krone, Marko said: "I subscribe to a saying by Mateschitz: 'We don't buy stars, we make stars'.

"We've always sought out our own drivers who are capable of winning a grand prix. With a few exceptions, it's worked.

"In keeping with that philosophy, the difficult decision between Liam Lawson and Nikola Tsolov at Racing Bulls should really go in Tsolov's favour."

title: Valtteri Bottas addresses Cadillac rumours with F1 future under threat
excerpt:
Valtteri Bottas holds a contract with Cadillac for the 2027 F1 season, but that does not mean the 10-time grand prix winner will definitely be racing for the American team.

Valtteri Bottas has dismissed speculation surrounding his F1 future at Cadillac, despite growing uncertainty over his position at the American team for 2027.

Bottas holds a contract for next season, but his performances relative to team-mate Sergio Perez have raised questions over whether Cadillac could make a change to its driver line-up.

Perez has consistently outperformed Bottas in the sister MAC-26, holding an 11-4 advantage in grands prix where both drivers have reached the chequered flag.

Although both drivers signed multi-year agreements when joining the new team, Cadillac team principal Marcin Budkowski has refused to guarantee that its current pairing will remain unchanged.

Speaking during the United States Grand Prix weekend, Budkowski acknowledged interest from drivers seeking opportunities for next season.

"As a team principal, and I'm sure it's the same with my colleagues, you're getting calls and contacts from every driver or driver manager that is on the market," Budkowski said in the team representatives' press conference on Friday.

"So, there are a number of drivers and managers who have contacted me. I'm not going to say who it is or who it isn't, but pretty much all of them that are on the market have been in touch, as you'd expect.

"But I think it's the last place [here in the press conference], as you can imagine, where I would communicate anything on the driver line-up. My marketing and communications department would kill me if I did that."

Asked about the contractual situation, he added: "Again, this is the last place I would comment on driver contracts, and in general, I think it's not something that is done in the press.

"It's something which will be done by official releases from the team when the time is right."

[Article continues below]

Bottas faces growing competition for Cadillac seat

As previously reported by RacingNews365, Esteban Ocon and his management have explored a potential move to Cadillac following confirmation of his departure from Haas.

The Frenchman previously worked with Budkowski at Alpine and could offer Cadillac another experienced grand prix winner.

Cadillac reserve driver Colton Herta is also under consideration, with the American manufacturer's owners keen on his potential.

Herta is closing in on the 40 superlicence points required to compete in F1, and Budkowski has confirmed the nine-time IndyCar winner has just one further point to claim, despite his underwhelming campaign in F2.

Yuki Tsunoda is another driver understood to be exploring an opportunity, having lost his Red Bull race seat last year, whilst Liam Lawson's representatives have also made exploratory contact amid uncertainty surrounding the New Zealander's Racing Bulls future.

Despite the growing interest, Cadillac is understood to be taking a cautious approach to any potential change.

Bottas, meanwhile, remains unconcerned by the speculation surrounding his future.

Asked whether the rumours were proving distracting after qualifying, the Finnish driver replied to media, including RacingNews365: "No, no.

"I've heard some rumours, but I know my situation, and it's all good. It's Formula 1. Everyone wants to be in Formula 1, so that's how it goes."

[Article continues below]

Bottas confident over Cadillac future

Bottas remained similarly unperturbed after the race, despite suffering a late retirement, his eighth of the season.

Asked whether he had received assurances over his place at Cadillac for 2027, the 10-time grand prix winner pointed to the terms of his existing agreement.

"Yes. I mean, last year when I signed, I know the terms, so that's all," he said.

Pressed on whether he could envisage any scenario in which he would not be racing for Cadillac next season, Bottas leaned on an old idiom to make his point.

"It is Formula 1, you know? If cows [pigs] could fly... Anything can always happen in this sport," he said.

"But for now, they seem happy with what they're getting out of me. So I think that's all that matters."

title: F2 champion gets fresh spate of F1 outings after 2027 plans announced
excerpt:
Leonardo Fornaroli will compete in FP1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix and also at the São Paulo Grand Prix for McLaren, having recently been confirmed as a driver for its Hypercar team next season.

The reigning F2 champion will deputise for Lando Norris at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, and for Oscar Piastri the following week at Interlagos.

"I am excited to be getting back into the MCL40 for the upcoming Free Practice 1 sessions in both Mexico City and São Paulo," Fornaroli said.

"They’re new circuits for me, which is a good challenge. Mexico presents new conditions for me to drive in with the altitude and low grip, with Brazil looking fun with the iconic features of the track.

"It is always a pleasure to work alongside the team at race weekends, so thank you to them for trusting me with further FP1 sessions."

The Italian had been in contention for a full-time seat in F1 with Haas, but fell short of current F2 standings leader Rafael Camara.

Nonetheless, Fornaroli will embark on an exciting new chapter with McLaren next term, alongside his F1 duties for the papaya squad.

By taking part in free practice 1 in Mexico City and Sao Paulo, in addition to runs in Barcelona and Budapest, Fornaroli will satisfy McLaren's FIA-mandated rookie FP1 criteria.

“Our preparations have been extensive. Alongside dedicated simulator work, I’ve done some Testing of Previous Cars running in last year’s double World Championship-winning car, which was an incredible experience," he added.

"That mileage provided good preparation for what lies ahead. My focus will be on helping the team set up Lando and Oscar’s cars and gathering a good bank of data. I am ready and eager to get out on circuit for both FP1 sessions."

title: McLaren still waiting for Lando Norris 'compensation'
excerpt:
Andrea Stella is convinced that what goes around comes around and McLaren and Lando Norris will receive payback for what happened in the Spanish GP.

Andrea Stella has said McLaren is still waiting for "compensation" for what happened to Lando Norris at the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid, with the team principal revisiting the saga after a one-stop gamble at the United States Grand Prix yielded fifth place for the Briton.

Norris finished fifth at the Circuit of the Americas, 30 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli, after McLaren opted against the conventional two-stop strategy in the hope of a safety car that never materialised.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Stella explained the thinking behind the call.

"We were actually catching up to the two Ferraris and [Max] Verstappen in the second stint, and at some stage we just decided to go for the one-stop," said Stella.

"Because if we go for a two-stop, we are always going to stay behind. For the one-stop, this gives you the possibility to take advantage of a safety car, which didn't come."

It was at that point that Stella returned to Madrid, where Norris lost out on victory to Antonelli despite starting on pole. An ill-timed virtual safety car played a cruel hand in denying Norris a win that would have been deserved.

"We are still waiting for compensation for what happened in Madrid? It will come," said Stella.

[Article continues below}

Stella pinpoints where improvement is needed

The Italian continued by detailing the layers of the strategy call in Austin, including a late look at whether the hard compound could be stretched to the finish - as was the case - behind both Ferraris and Verstappen's Red Bull.

"We also attempted to see what was left in the hard tyres. But honestly, we knew that it was very, very unlikely that we could have kept Verstappen and, in particular, Leclerc behind," said Stella.

"With Hamilton, we thought it was more dependent on the final tale of the hard tyres. Nobody would have known, but worthwhile giving it a go.

"So we are happy with the strategy execution; we are happy with the fact that we kind of understood which tyres needed to be used, and happy with the fact that the car seems to have improved thanks to the upgrades.

"But we need to improve our qualifying performance, and we also need to keep improving the car if we want to consistently compete for podiums, but above all for victories."

[Article continues below]

© XPB Images

Stella: Norris 'exaggerated a little bit'

That qualifying weakness was laid bare again in Austin, where Norris could only manage eighth on the grid, a second off Antonelli's pole time, before recovering ground in the race.

Stella suggested the result bore out McLaren's suspicion that the car's true pace was being masked on a single lap.

"In the race we saw that what we said [after qualifying] could have been the potential of the car was realised," he said. "We thought that we had a faster car than we were able to realise on track."

But the team boss pushed back on his driver's own assessment of what might have been possible in qualifying.

"Lando said that the car could have been good for P2," reflected Stella. " I think that's a little bit of an exaggeration because even if the potential was there, as I've explained, this year somehow is very difficult to use the full potential.

"It gets a little bit easier in the car in the race, because you don't push as much as you do in qualifying. You leave a little bit of margin.

"And the car was as competitive as the Ferraris and Red Bull, while Antonelli seemed to be a step ahead of everyone else."

title: George Russell offers F1 a solution for concerning driver issue
excerpt:
George Russell has suggested that F1 tracks be repaved every few years to avoid repeated concerns about bumpy surfaces.

The tarmac at the Circuit of the Americas, which hosts the United States Grand Prix, is known to be among the bumpiest throughout the year.

Four-time F1 drivers' champion Max Verstappen aimed criticism at the bumps at the venue, before and over the weekend, insisting it has resulted in damage to his spine.

There was even a back-and-forth between the Red Bull driver and chairman of COTA, Bobby Epstein, over the conditions.

Some, like Lewis Hamilton, downplayed the significance of the bumps, insisting he has not experienced the problems Verstappen spoke of.

The issue is more prevalent at the Austin circuit than at other tracks due to it being built on a marshland, but Russell indicated that vigorous care of the surface would stamp out the issue.

"Yeah, it's bumpy, but I think it's just part of racing, you know?" Russell told media including RacingNews365.

"I'd say my general view is, F1 tracks probably need to be repaved every couple of years just to make it a bit more consistent.

"Because we're going to tracks now where the tarmac is coming up and it's falling apart. It's causing more issues than not."

[Article continues below]

Why the issue is worse in F1

With F1 cars typically running so low to the ground compared to other categories in order to aid the production of downforce, Russell highlighted that they are much more sensitive to bumps.

"We're not an IndyCar or an F2 car that runs low ride heights reasonably high; our ride heights are 10 millimetres at the end of the straight — a centimetre from the ground," Russell added.

"So any tiny bump, you really feel it, and the side profile of the tyres now, since we've been with the 18-inch, is substantially smaller.

"The circumference of the tyre is the same. The circumference of the rim is far greater.

"You've lost all of that effective suspension in the tyre, which was a damper, which we kind of don't have anymore. So not ideal, but not much we can do."

title: Franco Colapinto steps aside at Alpine for F1 debutant in Mexico FP1
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto will sit out FP1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, with Alpine junior Gabriele Mini making his F1 debut at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

The Italian driver sits fourth in the F2 standings, just behind Alex Dunne, who is also part of Team Enstone's academy programme.

It marks the second time Colapinto has stepped aside for a free practice session in 2026, completing his FIA-mandated requirements for rookie drivers. Pierre Gasly in the other A526 still has one more session to surrender his car for.

Speaking ahead of the weekend in Mexico City, Mini said: "I'm looking forward to getting behind the wheel of the A526 and taking part in my first ever Free Practice 1 in Formula 1.

"Having been part of the Alpine Academy for several years and progressing through the junior ranks, competing in an official Formula 1 session is going to be a really special moment for me.

"Thank you to Flavio, Steve and everyone at the team for their trust and for the opportunity. I've been doing a lot of preparation back at base in Enstone, spending time on the simulator and working closely with the engineers to make sure I'm as ready as possible and able to put my best foot forward both personally and for the team.

"My goal is to do the best possible job on track and help provide valuable data and feedback to the team to hopefully set up a successful weekend, where both Pierre and Franco aim to score points by the end of it."

Mini will be joined by Freddie Slater, Jak Crawford, Luke Browning, Fred Vesti and Ayumu Iwasa in FP1, with Mexico City a popular venue for rookies to deputise.

Iwasa, who finished fourth in the F2 championship in 2023 and is the reigning Super Formula champion, has extensive experience from previous campaigns, too, having taken part in three FP1s last season and two the one before.

title: Isack Hadjar demands Red Bull fixes 'stupid little things' ruining F1 races
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has demanded that Red Bull find fixes for "stupid little things" which impacted his United States GP after a mixed weekend.

After a poor Friday, which he branded a "disaster" as he struggled for balance and feeling in the RB22, Hadjar rebounded to qualify in third place for the grand prix, 0.036s behind team-mate Max Verstappen in second.

In the race, a poor launch for Hadjar dropped him behind both Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, with the French racer also dropping behind Lando Norris's McLaren in the final results for a sixth-place finish.

His efforts were enough to see Red Bull leapfrog McLaren into third place in the constructors, with the two teams level on points, with Red Bull ahead on countback with four second places to McLaren's two, as both have 355 points and two grand prix wins apiece.

However, when asked for his reflections on the up-and-down Austin weekend, after his struggles on Friday and then third in qualifying, Hadjar declared that the team must "nail" the "stupid little things."

"Friday was a total mess, and my race pace was not good, and we turned some things around in FP3 and in qualifying, we had a good car," he began to media, including RacingNews365.

"The race pace [on Sunday] was good, and the hard part of it, we nailed, but the little stupid things, the little details, we need to nail them as well."

Adding further detail on these areas, Hadjar pinpointed the ongoing radio issues both cars are suffering from and the long-standing clutch and start problems.

"At the moment, it is the little things we can't do," he said.

"I have a poor radio; I don't even know what is happening. I drop the clutch, and it is a nightmare, so if we fix these two [issues], we might be on the podium.

"It is the hardest things it seems like we can do, and the silly things we can't."

[Article continues below]

Stuck in the wrong mode

Hadjar also revealed that following his pit-stop and move to the hard tyres, his RB22 machine became stuck in the wrong engine mode - something that was unable to be changed once he rejoined the race.

"Exiting the pits, I was stuck in the pit-stop throttle map, and you don't want to drive like that," he said.

"The pace on the hard was pretty good, but I was stuck with the pit-stop throttle map and from the second lap already, this was the issue.

"Honestly, what tyres [I had on] was the least of my issues, and I had a drivability problem, and then you can put the wet tyres on, and it is not going to change anything."

title: Honda declare upgrade 'roadmap' for big Aston Martin F1 boost
excerpt:
Honda has explained that it is targeting two big F1 upgrades for the 2027 season to bring a major boost to Aston Martin.

The new alliance has struggled with performance and reliability in 2026, with issues including a lack of power, severe vibrations, turbo lag, and drivability concerns.

Under the ADUO mechanism, Honda will be granted two upgrades for 2027 to allow it to try and catch up with other manufacturers; in a year, the power unit will be slightly tweaked to bring out more internal combustion power to reduce reliance on the battery systems.

Combustion is an area the engine has also struggled with, but chief engineer Shintaro Orihara is optimistic that twin upgrades, including one mid-2027, can bring the Japanese manufacturer, and thus Aston Martin, into line with its rivals.

"We need some steps to catch up to the top competitors, and our target is to bring some steps for round one [of 2027]," Orihara told media, including RacingNews365.

"But still, at round one, we can say we wouldn't be a top competitor, so we need one more step.

"So, as Adrian [Newey] has said, our target is to take another big step in the middle of the season, let's say maybe round eight [in Monaco].

"That is our roadmap, and we are working based on that roadmap.

"Our weak point is combustion, so we're working hard to improve our combustion, especially for next year, when [ICE] performance is more important compared to this year, so that is a key point for us."

[Article continues below]

Aston Martin back Honda

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack was then asked about the team potentially exploring a Red Bull Powertrains deal for 2028, should it decide to split from Honda.

However, he rejected the idea.

"I can only say that we have a partner, a long-term partner, which is Honda," he said.

"Which, by the way, has done its 500th race [in Austin], and I think we will be together when we win our first race together."

title: George Russell to miss crucial Mexico GP session in mandatory F1 absence
excerpt:
George Russell will miss Free Practice 1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, as team-mate Kimi Antonelli is on the cusp of the title.

For the first time in 2026, Russell will step out of the W17 for one of the two mandatory sessions he must give to a young driver - with Mercedes reserve Fred Vesti stepping into Russell's cockpit at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Antonelli had missed FP1 at the Barcelona-Catalunya and Hungarian Grands Prix earlier in the season to fulfil his two slots in favour of Vesti with Russell now required to miss one more session this year.

Mexico, owing to the dusty track conditions found in FP1, is a common place for drivers to miss one of their sessions and hand over to the younger driver before returning for FP2.

Russell must win the grand prix this weekend to have any hopes of beating Antonelli to the title, with the Italian holding a 123-point lead over the Briton, with 125 points remaining.

If Russell does not win, Antonelli will win the title by default, with Antonelli requiring a ninth-place finish if Russell does claim victory.

Lewis Hamilton also remains in contention, and if he also does not win, Antonelli is champion - with a 10th place sufficing should the seven-time champion win the race.

Vesti is not the only FP1 driver confirmed for Mexico thus far, with Aston Martin giving Jak Crawford a latest run-out, whilst Audi is to hand protege Freddie Slater his F1 weekend debut with his first FP1.

title: Red Bull explain 'painful' issue that will not be fixed until next F1 season
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has confirmed that the clutch problems plaguing the RB22 will not be resolved until next season, after Isack Hadjar called for a redesign following the United States Grand Prix.

Hadjar finished sixth at the Circuit of the Americas, but said after the race that the car's clutch assembly is "fragile" and struggles with operating temperatures, with start issues occurring that were not down to driver error.

Red Bull has endured launch problems throughout this campaign, with Max Verstappen and Hadjar regularly losing ground off the line compared to the frontrunners at Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes.

Speaking about the launch issues, Mekies said the problem touches almost every department at the team.

"The start is a slightly more complex issue to solve," said Mekies, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"The staff performance is going across pretty much all of the departments of the company, probably except aerodynamics. It's the engine, it's the gearbox, it's the clutch, it's many things.

"We have seen from the beginning of the season that we are not the benchmark in terms of launch performance. As much as we have reduced the gap to the competition, and you may remember how bad our starts were at the beginning of the year, we are still not the benchmark.

"The fact that the car in the meantime has improved a lot and is fighting closer to the front makes that deficit even more painful now because the competition around us is very strong.

"So, on one side, I'm confident that we will continue to reduce the gap to the competition from now to the end of the year because every race we learn, and every race we come up with small ways to close the gap.

"On the other side, I equally know that we will not be the benchmark before the end of the season, that it will require some significant design and hardware changes, and that this is something that we will only see next year."

[Article continues below]

Mekies - 'Truth in what Isack is saying'

Red Bull's weekend in Austin was also compromised by a separate problem: recurring radio dropouts that left Max Verstappen and Hadjar without pit instructions on occasion.

It marked the second consecutive race in which Red Bull's radio system had failed its drivers mid-session.

Mekies conceded that Hadjar's frustration, in particular, over the communication failures was justified.

"There is some truth in what Isack is saying, meaning we are all frustrated to struggle for the second race in a row with the radio issues," said Mekies. "It's making everyone's lives very difficult.

"It is true that it's something that we would like to fix quite quickly because it's an item that should be working without using too much of our energy, so he's right on that one.

"And if we understood it, we would have solved it, but we don't fully understand why we are being hit by these issues.

"I have to admit that the competition is doing a better job than us because we can obviously hear everyone's radio, and we have been struggling more than we would have liked to."

title: Carlos Sainz stunned by Arvid Lindblad penalty escape: 'Pretty nasty moment'
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has expressed surprise that Arvid Lindblad escaped a penalty for squeezing him against the pit wall at the start of the United States Grand Prix.

Fast-starting Williams driver Sainz tried to force his way through when faced with Lindblad's Racing Bulls ahead of him, only for the British driver to close the door on the Spaniard along the front straight, leading to him kissing the wall.

Sainz avoided serious contact but picked up front-wing damage in the process, which compromised his opening stint. The Spaniard was eventually forced to pit for a new nose that cost him several seconds, before recovering to finish 18th, one lap down.

Despite the severity of the squeeze, no investigation was opened, and Lindblad was not penalised by the stewards for the clash.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Sainz said his own race had started well before the incident unfolded.

"It was a good start," said Sainz. "We've picked up a trend now where I think everyone knows we're getting very good starts, and they kind of put us off a bit at the start always.

"I'm surprised he [Lindblad] got away with that because, obviously, he's putting someone in the wall and creating what could have potentially been a very big accident.

"I backed out in time, but I picked up a lot of front-wing damage, which compromised my first stint. On top of that, obviously a slow pit stop to change the front wing, seven, eight seconds extra, but then I managed to recover from there, and I settled down into a decent pace for the rest of the race.

"So yeah, bit of a shame at the start and that lap one was compromised, and stint one was compromised, but it is what it is."

[Article continues below]

Sainz - 'I've never got away with it'

The Williams driver went further when reflecting on the lack of sanction, questioning why the same standard did not appear to apply to him when he has been judged too aggressive in the past.

"We are all very high standards," said Sainz. "It's just that sometimes someone has a bit of an off moment, which always happens in F1.

"My opinion is that Arvid was maybe too much on me, but we've all been too much one or two days.

"What I'm surprised is that when you're too much, you get away with it. Whenever I've been too much, I've never got away with it.

"I'm surprised that someone got away with it because it was a pretty nasty moment there on the wall."
